newsitem.title: UK: Venezuela presses on with reform despite pain.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela presses on with reform despite pain.

text.p: Venezuela, riding high in the eyes of foreign investors as it implements a brace of swingeing IMF reforms, may miss its year-end inflation target but vowed on Tuesday to continue opening up its economy despite the pain. In London on three-day visit to meet foreign investors before heading home via Frankfurt and Paris, Venezuela's planning minister Teodoro Petkoff, a former communist guerrilla, said his government was fully committed to privatisation.
"The government is absolutely committed to privatisation. We had a set-back with Banco de Venezuela but we will continue with the process," he told Reuters in an interview.

"In November the phone company is coming to the markets. At the end of this year we have the aluminium sector, next year it will be the steel plants. Everything is going as established in the schedule," he said.

Investors were disappointed when the planned sell-off of Banco de Venezuela, valued at a minimum $275 million, fell through at the end of August despite the interest of banks from Germany, Spain, Colombia and Peru.
Petkoff said the government would make a second attempt this year, but stressed how difficult this transaction would be.
"It's not sewing and singing," he said.
Banco Consolidado, Banco Tequendama and Banco Latino are due on the privatisation block before December, and Banco Republica in the first quarter of 1997, he added.

In April, Caracas embarked on an IMF-backed reform programme which entailed gasoline price rises of 500 percent and lifting foreign exchange and interest rate controls. The aim was to slash an unweildy fiscal deficit and eliminate triple digit inflation.

But the measures brought with them 11.2 percent unemployment, negative real interest rates, and will push GDP growth this year down to negative three or four percent, though this should swing back to about 4.0 percent growth next year.
Petkoff said Venezuela was unlikely to achieve its monthly inflation target of 1.5 percent by December.

"The IMF still believes it can be reached. I myself think that it will be between 2.0 and 3.0 percent by the end of the year," he said. "But it will still be a fantastic performance compared with (12.6 percent in) May."

Petkoff was accompanied by central bank director Carlos Hernandez Delfino, who said the bank would continue soaking up the country's excess liquidity, which has been fuelling inflation, by issuing monetary stability bonds.
"As long as it is necessary to reduce (liquidity) the central bank will continue to place monetary stability bonds on the market," he said.

He said Venezuela's steady foreign exchange rate provided welcome stability despite negative real interest rates levels -- at 20 to 30 percent they are outweighed by near 100 percent annual inflation.

Windfall revenues from oil prices, driven higher by the current U.S. confontation with Iraq, have cushioned some of the effects of the reforms, but Petkoff said this would not push GDP growth into the positive zone this year.
He said he aimed to introduce a bill removing big severence payments for workers in the congressional session starting on October 1 following negotiations between business and labour.
But there was as yet no timetable for downsizing the central state administration, entailing substantial job losses.
Attempts to implement IMF-style reforms in 1989 sparked riots that left 300 dead. Petkoff said the lack of social unrest this time round was a tribute to the government's management.

"There are many reasons for people to be angry. This has been a heavy and severe programme, and to do that without riots and without social unrest means the government has managed the system in the right way," he said. "It is an achievement."
